records.name: Voldemārs
records.facts_used: Voldemārs: Klāvs Siliņš’s dictionary of Latvian personal names places Voldemārs under Valdemārs, whose entry explains the name through Old High German waltan, to rule, and māri, famous. Behind the Name likewise treats Voldemārs as the Latvian form of Valdemar, the Scandinavian form of German Waldemar; the same Germanic name was also used to translate the related Slavic Vladimir. These are glosses of the name’s parts, not a ready translation of the whole name. The dictionary records Voldemārs in Matīši in 1838 and dates its entry into the calendar to 1901. This is an early use recorded in the dictionary’s material, not proof of the first bearer in Latvia or of each family’s reason for the choice.
records.reason: Exact-form entry or explicit authoritative rendering bridge plus a dated record support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining element-level uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš p. 332 lists Voldemārs under Valdemārs (p. 315: waltan/māri); Matīši 1838, calendar 1901. Curated BTN Voldemārs = Latvian form of Valdemar; current BTN Waldemar gives walt + mari and only secondary use as a translation of Slavic Vladimir, which removes the earlier Germanic-versus-Slavic conflict. Date kept as an early record, not a first bearer.

records.name: Valdemārs
records.facts_used: Valdemārs: Klāvs Siliņš’s dictionary explains Valdemārs through Old High German waltan, to rule, and māri, famous. Behind the Name gives the same elements for German Waldemar and describes Scandinavian Valdemar as its form, also used to translate the related Slavic Vladimir. These glosses describe the name’s parts rather than a literal translation of every bearer’s name. records.name: Otīlija
records.facts_used: Otīlija: The Latvian Language Agency’s database pairs German Ottilie with Otīlija, and Behind the Name describes Ottilie as the German form of Odilia. Odilia is explained through the Old German element uodil, heritage, or ot, wealth or fortune, while Klāvs Siliņš’s dictionary gives Old High German othal, homeland. The sources agree on a Germanic origin but explain the exact first element differently. The German rendering is cited from L. Ceplītis’s 1960 guidance, page 63. Siliņš gives 1453 as the earliest possible attestation and dates the calendar entry to 1767; the source’s qualification ‘possible’ should be kept.
records.reason: Exact-form entry or explicit authoritative rendering bridge plus a dated record support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining element-level uncertainty is stated in the text.

records.name: Aivo
records.facts_used: Aivo: Wiktionary’s Estonian entry describes Aivo as a short form of Aivar, and Behind the Name calls Aivar the Estonian form of Ivar. Ivar goes back to Old Norse Ívarr, probably formed from elements meaning yew tree or bow and army or warrior. The meaning therefore belongs to the Scandinavian base, not to a separate Estonian word. The December 2005 issue of Leole, the Suure-Jaani parish newspaper, lists Aivo together with Aivar and derives both from Scandinavian Ivar. records.name: Ethel
records.facts_used: Ethel: Behind the Name explains Ethel as a short form of names beginning with Old English æðele, noble. It was coined in the nineteenth century, when many Old English names were revived. The spelling used in Estonia matches this English name, but the sources checked do not show when it entered Estonian use. EBSCO Research Starters dates William Makepeace Thackeray’s novel The Newcomes to 1853–1855 in serial form and 1855 as a book; one of its central figures is Ethel Newcome. This English literary example helped popularise the name and is not evidence about bearers in Estonia.
records.reason: Exact-form entry or explicit authoritative rendering bridge plus a dated record support two paragraphs in five languages; remaining element-level uncertainty is stated in the text.
records.uncertainties: Curated exact BTN Ethel: short form of names in Old English æðele noble, coined in the 19th century, popularised by The Newcomes (1855) and The Daisy Chain (1856). EBSCO Research Starters: The Newcomes serial 1853–1855, book 1855, character Ethel Newcome. No Estonian-specific entry date found; the earlier Adelheid same-day idea is not adopted.
